title: He Dumped an Entire Font into the Thames So No One Else Could Use It
dek: Over 173 nights, Thomas Cobden-Sanderson dumped 2,600 pounds of Doves Type into the Thames, because metal type is a physical object — dump it and you own it exclusively.
why: A narrative episode about a typeface, a broken friendship and revenge. The information density is low, but the story itself is intensely visual — good for a commute.
who: For listeners who like narrative podcasts and are interested in type design or Victorian publishing history — listen on the commute or while doing chores.
skip: The interview portion after 28:35 can be skipped; it's mostly about how the piece was made and is low on information.

points.h: Typeface stories always set listeners off
points.body: Roman Mars says up front that 99PI has done stories about architecture, transit, history and even sports, but stories about fonts and type always draw a flood of extremely passionate responses from listeners. This episode came out of a segment Helen Zaltzman and Martin Austwick developed for the live stage show Souvenirs, later adapted for radio.

points.h: Friends who live too close fall apart faster
points.body: Emery lived at 3 Hammersmith Terrace; in 1897 the Thomases moved to number 7 on the same street, and Emery even rented commercial space from Thomas. The two took family holidays together and stayed in adjoining cottages. In 1899 they decided to go further and start Doves Press as partners. Helen says they had been very important friends for more than a decade, but the relationship collapsed in only about two years.

points.h: Complementary skills couldn't save the partnership
points.body: Thomas was the perfectionist who cared only about the art of printing; Emery was the pragmatist who ran the business. On paper it was the perfect match, but it soured almost from the start. Thomas felt he did all the printing and proofreading himself, that Emery was hardly ever there, and that Emery never responded to his long arguments about how a letter should be designed. Emery, meanwhile, had another business to run and money to make, and no time to spend weeks or months with Thomas fussing over a single letter.

points.h: Type is a physical object, so ownership can be fought over
points.body: The split dragged on for seven years, and the core question was who owned Doves Type. At the time a typeface was thousands upon thousands of physical objects that couldn't be copied indefinitely — without that set of metal type, you didn't have that typeface. Thomas wanted it exclusively and didn't want Emery, or anyone else he couldn't control, printing anything in Doves. He offered a small sum for Emery to give up his rights; Emery wouldn't accept, and the tug-of-war went back and forth for years.

points.h: Dumping it in the river was a revenge seven years in the planning
points.body: Thomas throwing Doves Type into the Thames was not a sudden impulse. He waited seven years and wrote a 116-page apologia — the word doesn't mean an apology, it means a defense. He had wanted to publish it in 1913, but realized it might incriminate him, so he kept waiting, until he was about to shut down Doves Press and print its last book, and only then, on an evening in August 1916, did he act.

points.h: 173 nights, at most 15 pounds at a time
points.body: Thomas could carry at most 10 to 15 pounds of type at a time, and the full set weighed at least 2,600 pounds. By that math he made at least 173 trips to the bridge. Each night he wrapped the type from the page he had just printed in white paper, bagged it, stuffed it into his pockets or into a wooden toolbox with a sliding lid, and sprinkled it gently off the bridge — he didn't want a splash, and he didn't want to be seen. He was afraid of being caught, because the type had legally been promised to Emery.

points.h: Nearly a century later, someone found it on the riverbed
points.body: Emery had asked the original engraver, Edward Prince, to remake Doves Type, but Prince was nearly eighty and his eyes and hands could no longer do such fine work. Then in 2010 the type designer Robert Green began redrawing it. He spent three years making a digital version, wasn't satisfied with it, and in 2014 went himself to the exposed riverbed under Hammersmith Bridge at low tide, where within 20 minutes he found a lowercase v, and then with a dive team found 151 pieces of Doves Type in all.

points.h: Whoever leaves more writing controls the narrative
points.body: Helen says Thomas left behind a huge quantity of letters and diaries, while Emery's letters are far fewer, so Thomas had a stronger grip on the narrative. For decades people assumed Emery was the jerk, because he complained less. In the diaries of his last forty years, Thomas edited Emery out entirely, and when Annie published those diaries on the fourth anniversary of his death, Emery wasn't in them.

quotes.text: But one kind of story that always elicits a huge response from a very vocal constituency are stories about type.
after at least a decade of friendship, in 1899 you decided to take your relationship to the next level. You set up a printing press together.
And if you didn't have the type, then you didn't have the type.
Throwing something away into a body of water sounds spontaneous, doesn't it?
Let's not forget, the word apologia does not mean an apology. It's a defence argument.
Metal that you loved so much, you must destroy it rather than let it live without you.
A hole where a memory used to be is still a memory-shaped hole.
